ending: Under Dr. Nolan's humane care at the private hospital, Esther slowly climbs out of her breakdown through insulin treatment and a course of properly administered electroshock that finally lifts the crushing weight of her depression. She begins to reclaim a sense of control over her own life, most pointedly by being fitted for a diaphragm and then losing her virginity to a man named Irwin, an encounter that leaves her hemorrhaging badly and needing medical help. Her fellow patient Joan Gilling, a woman from her past who had also known Buddy Willard, appears to be improving but then hangs herself, and Esther attends her funeral. As the novel closes, Esther, much recovered and released from many of her old illusions, waits to be interviewed by the hospital board before returning to college. She steps toward the door uncertain of the future and conscious that the bell jar of madness might one day close over her again, but for now free of it and ready to go on. Buddy visits and their romance is plainly over.
in_short: Esther Greenwood, a brilliant college student, spends a summer as a guest editor at a New York fashion magazine but feels numb and disconnected amid its glamour, disillusioned with the expectations placed on young women and with her conventional suitor Buddy Willard. Returning home to Massachusetts, she learns she has been rejected from a writing course and sinks into a severe depression, unable to sleep, read, or write. An incompetent psychiatrist subjects her to a traumatic electroshock treatment, and her despair deepens until she attempts suicide by swallowing sleeping pills and hiding in a crawlspace. Found alive after several days, she is hospitalized and eventually transferred, through the help of a wealthy benefactor, to a private hospital under the care of the compassionate Dr. Nolan. There, with insulin therapy and properly managed electroshock, she gradually recovers. A fellow patient and acquaintance, Joan Gilling, hangs herself, and Esther, having taken new steps toward independence, prepares to leave the hospital and resume her life, cautiously hopeful but aware that the suffocating bell jar of her illness could descend again.

recaps.text: Esther Greenwood, a talented scholarship student, has won a month in New York as one of a dozen college girls guest-editing a fashion magazine, staying at a women's hotel and swept through luncheons, photo shoots, and parties. Instead of the excitement she is supposed to feel, she is increasingly numb and estranged from it all. She is pulled between two fellow interns: the cynical, glamorous Doreen, who flouts the program's rules and chases nightlife, and the wholesome, conventional Betsy. A magazine banquet leaves the group with food poisoning, and encounters with the driven editor Jay Cee and a courteous United Nations interpreter push Esther to brood on her future and on what a woman is expected to want. Threaded through these New York days are her memories of her medical-student suitor Buddy Willard, whose hypocrisy about sex and smug conventionality have soured her on him and on the settled married life he represents, deepening her sense that she does not fit the roles laid out for her.

Esther's New York month ends bleakly, and she returns home to the Boston suburbs only to learn she has been rejected from a summer writing course she was counting on. With the structure of her ambitions knocked away, she spirals into a deepening depression: she cannot sleep, cannot read or write, and stops washing or changing her clothes, while her anxious mother urges ordinary cheer she cannot summon. Sent to the complacent psychiatrist Dr. Gordon, she is given a badly handled electroshock treatment that terrifies and further isolates her. Her thoughts turn obsessively to death, and she circles various methods before finally swallowing a bottle of sleeping pills and crawling into a hidden space beneath the house. She is discovered still alive after several days and hospitalized. Through the intervention of the wealthy novelist Philomena Guinea, who once funded her scholarship, she is moved to a private hospital, where the sympathetic Dr. Nolan takes charge of her care and a more humane course of treatment begins.

At the private hospital, under Dr. Nolan's steady and compassionate guidance, Esther slowly recovers through insulin therapy and, crucially, a course of properly administered electroshock that at last lifts the smothering weight of her depression. She regains a foothold in reality and begins to assert control over her own life, including being fitted for a diaphragm as a step toward independence and then losing her virginity to a mathematics professor named Irwin, an encounter that leaves her bleeding dangerously and needing to be rushed for help. A fellow patient, Joan Gilling, a young woman from Esther's hometown who had also been tied to Buddy Willard, seems to be getting better but then hangs herself, and Esther goes to her funeral. Buddy visits, and it is clear their relationship is finished. As the book ends, Esther, greatly improved and stripped of many old illusions, waits to be interviewed by the hospital board before leaving to resume her studies. She walks toward the meeting uncertain but alive and hopeful, aware that the bell jar that once sealed her off could someday descend again, yet for now released from it.
